desc:
You are given a binary tree whose node values are distinct but not necessarily ordered. In one operation you may pick any two nodes and swap their values; the shape of the tree never changes.

Return the minimum number of operations needed to make the tree a valid binary search tree (for every node, all values in its left subtree are smaller and all values in its right subtree are larger).

Tree encoding. A binary tree is written as an integer array in level order. The first entry is the root. After that, the left and right child of every existing node are written in turn, level by level, from left to right. A missing child is written as -1 (real node values are never negative, so -1 cannot be confused with a value). Missing nodes have no children listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped. The empty tree is [].

For example, [5,2,7,-1,3,6] is the tree whose root 5 has left child 2 and right child 7; node 2 has no left child and right child 3; node 7 has left child 6 and no right child.

Example 1

tree = [3,2,1]
Output: 2
The inorder sequence is 2,3,1 and must become 1,2,3. Swap the values 2 and 1, then 3 and 2 – two swaps are needed.

Example 2

tree = [4,2,6,1,3,5,7]
Output: 0
hints: For a fixed tree shape, which value must end up in which node? Think about what order an inorder traversal must produce.

The tree is a BST exactly when its inorder sequence is sorted increasing, and the shape fixes the inorder positions. So the target arrangement is unique: the sorted values placed in inorder positions.

The task becomes: the minimum number of swaps to sort the inorder array of distinct numbers. Map every element to its rank, view the array as a permutation, and count cycles: the answer is n - (number of cycles).
editorial: Because the shape is fixed and a BST's inorder traversal is strictly increasing, the final tree is completely determined: the k-th smallest value goes to the k-th node in inorder. Swapping values of two nodes is swapping two entries of the inorder array, so we need the minimum number of swaps that sorts that array.

Replace each value by its rank (position in sorted order). The array is then a permutation, which decomposes into cycles; a cycle of length L needs exactly L-1 swaps and no swap can do better than merging one cycle fix per swap. Hence the answer is n - cycles. Time is O(n log n) for the sort, space O(n).
